profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Louisville - East) is located at 2101 Nelson Miller Parkway, Louisville, KY 40223. The operator publishes a footprint of 33588 square feet and 1.46 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. Kentucky utility LG&E and KU reported in May 2026 that as many as 30 data center projects were under discussion statewide, with 11 having at least a 50% probability of proceeding and requiring roughly 3.5 gigawatts of electricity, enough to power more than 2 million homes; the parent company's CEO said total prospective demand could reach around 12 gigawatts, against Kentucky's maximum generation capacity of 18.4 gigawatts as of summer 2024, per Kentucky Lantern's reporting. LG&E and KU identified four data center projects as "imminent," at roughly 80% probability, including a planned development in West Louisville. Kentucky lawmakers have offered sales-tax incentives for data centers but had not, as of 2026, enacted regulatory protections requiring the facilities to fund their own dedicated infrastructure; a GOP-backed bill to require that funding failed during the 2026 legislative session.

Separate from Flexential's existing colocation footprint, Louisville is set to host Kentucky's first hyperscale data center campus, a 153-acre, seven-building project on Camp Ground Road near Shively developed by PowerHouse Data Centers and Poe Companies, described as a several-billion-dollar investment; power demand is projected to reach 400 megawatts, with an initial 130 MW targeted by October 2026 and LG&E building a dedicated switch station for the project. Louisville's Planning Commission approved the project 6-1 in March 2026 over objections from more than 20 residents who cited pollution and grid-strain concerns in the historically industrial Rubbertown-adjacent area; because current code classifies large data centers as a "telecommunications hotel" use, the project did not require Metro Council rezoning approval. In response, Louisville Metro has drafted a size-tiered data center zoning ordinance limiting facilities to 500,000 square feet, requiring conditional-use permits and setbacks of 200 to 500 feet from homes, schools, and hospitals for mid-size and large facilities, and banning co-located gas turbines; the draft drew more than 3,600 public comments ahead of a Planning Commission vote scheduled for September 3, 2026.

reading.body:
Flexential Louisville - East publishes 1.46 MW of IT capacity, modest enough to support roughly 37 racks at AI training density, and does not indicate large-scale AI infrastructure.

The facility occupies 33,588 square feet of technical space. At 10 kW per rack, a standard colocation density, that capacity supports approximately 146 racks. At 40 kW per rack, typical of AI training clusters, it supports roughly 37 racks. These are assumptions about rack density based on industry norms, not operator specifications. The footprint and published load suggest a general-purpose colocation campus rather than infrastructure built for compute-intensive AI workloads.

The certification stack reflects the workloads this facility is built to serve. SOC 1 Type II and SOC 2 Type II attest to financial and operational controls. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment card systems. ITAR qualifies it for export-controlled defense and aerospace data. NIST 800-53 and HITRUST together cover federal security and healthcare compliance requirements. These certifications position the facility for regulated enterprise workloads, including AI deployments in healthcare, defense, or financial services that require adjacent compliance infrastructure alongside compute capacity.

In Kentucky's mapped data center footprint, this facility ranks third by published IT capacity among facilities that disclose megawatt figures. The state's three reporting facilities total 9.55 MW, of which this campus represents 1.46 MW. That regional contribution is not a constraint on or enabler of AI scaling. This data covers only what operators have published and does not represent the full picture of Kentucky's data center market or its role in larger power and compute networks.
